items.title: In UP, arithmetic alone won’t make an opposition alliance
items.summary: With the Uttar Pradesh assembly polls due early next year, alliance-making is the first job for every party in the fray. The opposition is already feeling the strain, and its worry is that the noise will grow. The SP has also begun naming candidates while talks are still on, which has left Congress wondering how serious its partner is about a joint fight. In essence, the disagreement reflects competing assessments of electoral strength and the future shape of the opposition. items.title: Justice constrained to legal formality: Pushing citizens back to the law of Karma
items.summary: Over the course of history, the sovereign has actively assumed the responsibility of guaranteeing justice among its citizens. By doing so, the State consciously rejected the notion of justice based solely on the ‘Law of Karma', thereby discarding the ancient divine theory of justice , which assumes that a Creator or supernatural power will automatically dispense retribution and reward the righteous. By establishing structured adjudicatory mechanisms, statutory frameworks and enforcement agencies, the modern State sought to replace justice left to destiny with justice delivered by law. items.title: DMK backs delimitation Bill, says key demands addressed
items.summary: The DMK's decision to support the revised delimitation Bill has opened up a fresh political debate in Tamil Nadu. The party, which had strongly opposed the proposed exercise over concerns that southern states could lose parliamentary representation because of their population control measures, has now announced its support for the revised proposal. However, the decision has drawn criticism from political opponents, including the ruling TVK, who accuse the DMK of abandoning its earlier opposition to delimitation. DMK leaders have defended the decision, arguing that rejecting the revised proposal could leave Tamil Nadu to a future population-based delimitation exercise following the 2027 Census and warn that the state's representation could instead fall from 39 to 31 seats.

items.title: What the delimitation fight means and why this time is different
items.summary: Seven months after its delimitation plan was voted down, the government is trying again. Parliament reconvenes on Monday for a four-day sitting on a question India has put off for half a century: how many Lok Sabha seats each state should get. Seat shares have been frozen at 1971 population figures since 1976. That freeze lapses once the next census is published, and the government wants the terms settled before then. The April bill, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, would have raised the Lok Sabha’s maximum strength from 543 to 850 and tied the expansion to the 33 percent reservation for women. It fell short of a two-thirds majority, 298 votes to 230 against the 352 it needed, and the government withdrew the accompanying Delimitation Bill, 2026. This time, the Union Cabinet has approved a different bill. The Constitution Bill (132nd Amendment) would write a uniform 50 percent increase in every state’s seats into the Constitution, raise the cap on the Lok Sabha to 850, and extend the freeze on each state’s share of seats to 2051. The university will use it for legal research, academic writing, coursework and moot court preparation. At the centre of the adoption is Academic Mode, 8rney’s workspace for law schools. It supports students and researchers through each stage of a project: framing a research question, finding and analysing legal materials, developing arguments, and drafting and structuring papers, dissertations and assignments. Faculty can also use it for their own research. About implementing agentic legal intelligence at RGNUL, Professor (Dr.) Jai S. Singh , Vice-Chancellor, RGNUL said, “Research and advocacy have always been at the heart of legal education at RGNUL, in our classrooms and in moot court. AI is becoming part of legal practice, and our students should learn to use it well before they enter the profession. With 8rney, our students and faculty have tools that support rigorous research, writing and moot preparation, while legal reasoning and analysis remain at the centre of how we teach.” 8rney is co-founded by Aryaman Singh

items.title: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty: Jharkhand High Court Chief Justice MS Sonak at farewell
items.summary: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty and should be willing to accept criticism, Jharkhand High Court Chief Justice Mahesh Sharadchandra Sonak said on Friday. Justice Sonak was speaking at an event held to mark his retirement from judicial service. He was elevated as an Additional Judge of the Bombay High Court in June 2013 and served there for nearly 13 years before taking over as Chief Justice of the Jharkhand High Court in January 2026. In his farewell address, he expressed his discomfort with the practice of praising judges for performing their judicial duties. "I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising the judges for doing their judicial duties. No one deserves praise for doing what he or she ought to do. Just as Oliver Wendell Holmes once bemoaned that the trouble with most of us is that we would rather be ruined by praise than be saved by criticism," said Justice Sonak. items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently restored Mumbai traders’ registration of the ‘Le Shark’ trademark, a year after a single-judge ordered its removal on a rectification plea filed by UK-based company Le Shark Apparel Limited [Anil Shah Trading as Le Shark India (India) & Anr v. Le Shark Apparel Ltd & Ors] A Division Bench of Justices Bharati Dangre and Ashish S Chavan set aside the single-judge bench judgment that had allowed UK-based Le Shark Apparel's rectification plea under Sections 47 and 57 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. The Division Bench noted that the Trade Marks Act operates territorially and does not recognise extra-territorial use of a trademark as conferring enforceable rights in India unless such use translates into legally protectable goodwill in the Indian market. The Court noted that there was not a single pleading to suggest that the UK-based company had business presence in India. "The petitioner ‘Le Shark Apparel’ has not produced on record any evidence to demonstrate its business presence in India and admittedly whatever data is furnished in the rectification application in relation to its registration, including sales, etc. is exclusively outside India," the Court
